newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-BAA profit hit by T5 write-off.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-BAA profit hit by T5 write-off.

text.p: Profits growth at airport operator BAA Plc could be overshadowed by delays in getting approval to build a giant new fifth terminal at London Heathrow when it reports on Monday, analysts said.
Profits before exceptionals are expected to be up 11 percent at around 450 million stg for the year to March 31, compared to 403 million pounds last year.

But a write-off on some of the preparatory costs for the 1.5 billion stg Terminal Five project will push down the pre-tax result, and an exceptional property gain pushed up the pre-tax result last year to 418 million stg.

BAA announced in April that delays in the protracted public planning inquiry for Terminal Five had forced the company to stop capitalising interest on preparatory expenditure, although it would continue to capitalise the costs themselves.

As a result, it said, it would book in a 40 million exceptional interest charge in the results to write off the accumulated interest previously capitalised. It said it would also be increasing its interest charges for the year just ended by 13 million stg.
Primarily, the move was seen as an act of financial prudency, prompted by concerns that BAA was capitalising interest on a project which had not yet been approved.

But some analysts suspect in the timing that BAA might also have been encouraged to act now and depress profits by the prospect of the new Labour government's proposed windfall tax on excess profits made by privatised utilities.

BAA denies it has been making excess profits since it was privatised 10 years ago and should not be liable. But Labour has refused to identify target companies ahead of Chancellor Gordon Brown's budget on July 2.

Analysts say BAA's underlying business is performing well, with traffic at BAA's seven British airports up again last year by 4.6 percent at 98 million passengers, fuelling demand in BAA's airport shopping complexes.
"We like BAA. It's a good mix of risk and reward," said Chris Tarry, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, who predicts that traffic growth would go on growing.
But other analysts said the accounting changes could aggravate concerns over delays to Terminal Five, designed to increase capacity at Heathrow by nearly 50 percent to 80 million passengers a year.
"The stock is quite fairly valued. But I think the delay in the terminal is not yet in the price", said transport analyst Marshall Whiting of SocGen.
The longer Terminal Five is delayed the more money BAA could be forced to spend on temporary solutions to avert congestion both in air traffic and in handling passengers, Whiting said.
